claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) ESX-1 protein secretion system mediates phagosomal membrane damage.
source: The Mtb ESX-1 protein secretion system has long been known to mediate phagosomal membrane damage (Manzanillo et al., 2012; Simeone et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Manzanillo et al., 2012 and Simeone et al., 2012

claim: The mycobacterial lipid PDIM plays a role in phagosomal membrane damage during infection.
source: the mycobacterial lipid PDIM was more recently found to play a similar role in infection (Augenstreich et al., 2017; Barczak et al., 2017; Quigley et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Augenstreich et al., 2017; Barczak et al., 2017; Quigley et al., 2017

claim: Wild-type Mtb strain H37Rv, PDIM mutants, and ESX-1 mutants are taken up at similar rates into bone marrow-derived macrophages.
source: using either CFU or flow cytometry we found that wild-type Mtb strain H37Rv, PDIM mutants, and ESX-1 mutants were taken up at similar rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B using CFU and flow cytometry measurements

claim: 907 genes changed two-fold upon infection of BMDM with wild-type Mtb.
source: Focusing on the 907 genes changed two-fold upon infection, genes could be categorized into three clusters with distinct patterns of expression (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: Cluster 1 genes were progressively induced over time after infection with wild-type Mtb.
source: Cluster 1 genes were progressively induced, and cluster 2 genes were progressively repressed over time after infection
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data showing temporal expression patterns

claim: Cluster 2 genes were progressively repressed over time after infection with wild-type Mtb.
source: Cluster 1 genes were progressively induced, and cluster 2 genes were progressively repressed over time after infection
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data showing temporal expression patterns

claim: Cluster 3 genes were induced upon infection and peaked at 8–12 hr before waning.
source: Cluster 3 genes were induced upon infection and peaked at 8–12 hr before waning
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data showing temporal expression patterns

claim: Expression of genes in cluster 1 was markedly impacted by loss of PDIM or ESX-1.
source: In contrast, expression of genes in cluster 1 was markedly impacted by loss of PDIM or ESX-1
evidence: Supported by comparison of RNAseq data between wild-type and mutant infections

claim: Cluster 1 genes can be divided into two subclusters (1A and 1B) based on their response to PDIM and ESX-1 mutants.
source: classifying genes in this cluster based on their response to PDIM and ESX-1 mutants clearly distinguished two subclusters (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: Induction of genes in subcluster 1A was markedly diminished in response to PDIM and ESX-1 mutants relative to wild-type Mtb.
source: Induction of genes in subcluster 1A was markedly diminished in response to PDIM and ESX-1 mutants relative to wild-type Mtb (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Subcluster 1A genes comprise the type I IFN response.
source: Ingenuity pathway analysis (Krämer et al., 2014) of genes in this subcluster predicted STAT1, IRF3, IFN, and IFNAR as upstream regulators with high confidence, suggesting that these genes comprised the type I IFN response
evidence: Supported by Ingenuity pathway analysis and manual inspection confirming IFN stimulated genes

claim: The macrophage type I IFN response to Mtb is dependent upon ESX-1-mediated secretion.
source: These results were consistent with previous work demonstrating that the macrophage type I IFN response to Mtb is dependent upon ESX-1-mediated secretion (Stanley et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Stanley et al., 2007 and consistency with current data

claim: The macrophage type I IFN response to Mtb is dependent upon PDIM.
source: These results were consistent with previous work demonstrating that the macrophage type I IFN response to Mtb is dependent upon ESX-1-mediated secretion (Stanley et al., 2007) and PDIM (Barczak et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Barczak et al., 2017 and consistency with current data

claim: Expression of genes in subcluster 1B was enhanced in response to PDIM or ESX-1 mutants relative to wild-type Mtb at later timepoints.
source: In contrast to subcluster 1A, expression of genes in subcluster 1B was enhanced in response to PDIM or ESX-1 mutants relative to wild-type Mtb at later timepoints (Figures 1C–D–2A)
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figures 1C, 1D, and 2A

claim: Subcluster 1B includes Marco, a gene important for the host response to Mtb.
source: Strikingly, this subcluster included multiple genes important for the host response to Mtb, including Marco (Bowdish et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bowdish et al., 2013

claim: Subcluster 1B includes prostaglandin E synthase, a gene important for the host response to Mtb.
source: Strikingly, this subcluster included multiple genes important for the host response to Mtb, including Marco (Bowdish et al., 2013), prostaglandin E synthase (Chen et al., 2008; Garg et al., 2008; Mayer-Barber et al., 2014; Rangel Moreno et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2008; Garg et al., 2008; Mayer-Barber et al., 2014; Rangel Moreno et al., 2002

claim: Subcluster 1B includes lipocalin 2, a gene important for the host response to Mtb.
source: Strikingly, this subcluster included multiple genes important for the host response to Mtb, including Marco (Bowdish et al., 2013), prostaglandin E synthase (Chen et al., 2008; Garg et al., 2008; Mayer-Barber et al., 2014; Rangel Moreno et al., 2002), lipocalin 2 (Guglani et al., 2012; Saiga et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Guglani et al., 2012; Saiga et al., 2008

claim: Subcluster 1B includes Irg1, a gene important for the host response to Mtb.
source: Strikingly, this subcluster included multiple genes important for the host response to Mtb, including Marco (Bowdish et al., 2013), prostaglandin E synthase (Chen et al., 2008; Garg et al., 2008; Mayer-Barber et al., 2014; Rangel Moreno et al., 2002), lipocalin 2 (Guglani et al., 2012; Saiga et al., 2008), Irg1 (Hoffmann et al., 2019; Nair et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2019; Nair et al., 2018

claim: Subcluster 1B includes matrix metalloproteinase 14, a gene important for the host response to Mtb.
source: Strikingly, this subcluster included multiple genes important for the host response to Mtb, including Marco (Bowdish et al., 2013), prostaglandin E synthase (Chen et al., 2008; Garg et al., 2008; Mayer-Barber et al., 2014; Rangel Moreno et al., 2002), lipocalin 2 (Guglani et al., 2012; Saiga et al., 2008), Irg1 (Hoffmann et al., 2019; Nair et al., 2018), and matrix metalloproteinase 14 (Sathyamoorthy et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sathyamoorthy et al., 2015

claim: The kinetics of overall induction and enhanced expression observed in response to the PDIM and ESX-1 mutants were independent of MOI.
source: The kinetics of overall induction and enhanced expression observed in response to the PDIM and ESX-1 mutants were independent of MOI, as the same patterns were observed infecting with MOI 2:1 and 10:1 (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B comparing different MOIs

claim: Enhanced expression of subcluster 1B genes was similarly elicited in BALB/c BMDM.
source: Enhanced expression was similarly elicited in BALB/c BMDM, suggesting that the enhanced response is independent of the background genetic inflammatory state of the cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Enhanced expression of subcluster 1B genes was observed regardless of the specific PDIM or ESX-1 mutation.
source: Enhanced expression was observed regardless of the specific PDIM or ESX-1 mutation, including ESX-1 core complex mutant Tn::eccCa1, secreted effector mutants (esxB and Tn::espC), mutants in the synthetic pathway for distinct components of PDIM (mas and ppsD), and a PDIM transport mutant (Tn::drrC) (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C testing multiple mutants

claim: Complementation of the disrupted ESX-1 or PDIM gene restored expression to wild-type levels.
source: Complementation of the disrupted ESX-1 or PDIM gene restored expression to wild-type levels (Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: PDIM and ESX-1 mutants are attenuated for growth in macrophages.
source: PDIM and ESX-1 mutants are both known to be attenuated for growth in macrophages (Camacho et al., 1999; Stanley et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Camacho et al., 1999 and Stanley et al., 2003

claim: The pckA mutant is highly attenuated for growth in macrophages.
source: The deleted gene, pckA, catalyzes the first step in gluconeogenesis, and the mutant is highly attenuated for growth in macrophages (Marrero et al., 2010; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by citation to Marrero et al., 2010 and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Infection with the pckA mutant did not elicit enhanced expression of subcluster 1B genes.
source: Infection with the pckA mutant did not elicit enhanced expression of subcluster 1B genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: The enhanced response to PDIM or ESX-1 mutants is not a general response to mutants with impaired intracellular survival.
source: Infection with the pckA mutant did not elicit enhanced expression of subcluster 1B genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that the enhanced response to PDIM or ESX-1 mutants is not a general response to mutants with impaired intracellular survival
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing pckA mutant with PDIM and ESX-1 mutants

claim: Ingenuity pathway analysis of genes in subcluster 1B predicted MYD88 and NF-κB as upstream regulators.
source: Ingenuity pathway analysis of genes in subcluster 1B predicted MYD88 and NF-κB as upstream regulators
evidence: Supported by Ingenuity pathway analysis of RNAseq data

claim: Expression of subcluster 1B genes in response to either wild-type Mtb or the mutants was lost in Myd88-/- BMDM.
source: Consistent with pathway predictions, expression in response to either wild-type Mtb or the mutants was lost in Myd88-/- BMDM (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Expression of representative subcluster 1B genes upon infection with wild-type Mtb or PDIM or ESX-1 mutants was entirely lost in Tlr2-/- BMDM.
source: Similar to findings for MYD88, expression of representative genes upon infection with wild-type Mtb or PDIM or ESX-1 mutants was entirely lost in Tlr2-/- BMDM (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Tlr4-/- knockout BMDM responded similarly to wild-type BMDM for subcluster 1B genes.
source: In contrast, Tlr4-/- knockout BMDM responded similarly to wild-type BMDM (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: MYD88 and TLR2 are upstream regulators of the macrophage transcriptional response component blunted by PDIM and ESX-1 function.
source: These results confirmed MYD88 and TLR2 as upstream regulators of macrophage transcriptional response component blunted by PDIM and ESX-1 function
evidence: Supported by experimental data from knockout BMDM experiments

claim: Tnf did not cluster with 1B genes; instead Tnf was in cluster 3.
source: Tnf did not cluster with 1B genes; instead Tnf was in cluster 3 (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: Expression of Tnf peaked earlier post-infection than expression of subcluster 1B genes and then waned.
source: Our RNAseq data additionally demonstrated that expression of Tnf peaked earlier post-infection than expression of subcluster 1B genes and then waned
evidence: Supported by RNAseq temporal expression data

claim: Tnf expression was very modestly impacted by PDIM and ESX-1.
source: At both MOI 2:1 and 10:1, we found that Tnf expression was very modestly impacted by PDIM and ESX-1 (Figure 3C–D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C–D

claim: Tnf expression was partially lost in Tlr2-/- and Myd88-/- BMDM.
source: Tnf expression was partially lost in Tlr2-/- and Myd88-/- BMDM (Figure 3E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Additional PRRs likely contribute to Tnf expression in response to Mtb.
source: Tnf expression was partially lost in Tlr2-/- and Myd88-/- BMDM (Figure 3E), suggesting that additional PRRs likely contribute to Tnf expression in response to Mtb
evidence: Inferred from partial loss of Tnf expression in knockout cells

claim: 17 genes have expression highly correlated with Tnf across all infection conditions.
source: clustering genes across all infection conditions identified 17 genes with expression highly correlated with Tnf (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Nfkbiz expression was minimally impacted by PDIM and ESX-1.
source: Similar to Tnf, expression was minimally impacted by PDIM and ESX-1 and was partially dependent upon MYD88 and TLR2 (Figure 3C–E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C–E

claim: TNF release upon Mtb infection was partially dependent upon MYD88 and TLR2.
source: However, we found that similar to Tnf transcription, TNF release upon Mtb infection was partially dependent upon MYD88 and TLR2 (Figure 3F)
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3F

claim: TNF release was very modestly increased upon infection with PDIM- or ESX-1-mutant Mtb.
source: However, we found that similar to Tnf transcription, TNF release upon Mtb infection was partially dependent upon MYD88 and TLR2 (Figure 3F) and very modestly increased upon infection with PDIM- or ESX-1-mutant Mtb (Figure 3G)
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Mtb infection of macrophages induces distinct early and late TLR2-dependent transcriptional responses.
source: Our results thus suggest that Mtb infection of macrophages induces distinct early and late TLR2-dependent transcriptional responses, and that canonical Mtb virulence factors that interfere with phagosomal membrane integrity preferentially blunt the later response
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental data showing temporal differences in TLR2-dependent gene expression

claim: Canonical Mtb virulence factors that interfere with phagosomal membrane integrity preferentially blunt the later TLR2-dependent response.
source: Our results thus suggest that Mtb infection of macrophages induces distinct early and late TLR2-dependent transcriptional responses, and that canonical Mtb virulence factors that interfere with phagosomal membrane integrity preferentially blunt the later response
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental data showing differential effects of PDIM and ESX-1 on early vs late responses

claim: Treatment with PAM3CSK4 elicited expression of genes in the early component of the TLR2-dependent response to Mtb with a similar pattern of expression, peaking at 2–4 hr post-treatment before waning.
source: Treatment with either synthetic ligand elicited expression of genes in the early component of the TLR2-dependent response to Mtb with a similar pattern of expression, peaking at 2–4 hr post-treatment before waning (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: PAM3CSK4 elicited expression of genes in the later TLR2-dependent response component with delayed kinetics, evident by 4 hr post-infection but continuing to increase through 24 hr.
source: PAM3CSK4 or PAM2CSK4 also elicited expression of genes in the later TLR2-dependent response component with delayed kinetics, evident by 4 hr post-infection but continuing to increase through 24 hr (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Synthetic ligand-dependent expression of genes representative of both the early and late clusters was dependent upon TLR2 and the signaling adapter MYD88.
source: As with Mtb infection, synthetic ligand-dependent expression of genes representative of both the early and late clusters was dependent upon TLR2 and the signaling adapter MYD88 (Figure 4C–D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C–D

claim: Treating BMDM with purified PIM6 induced the early and late response genes in a TLR2-dependent manner.
source: PIM6 has been described to be the most potent TLR2 agonist in the Mtb PAMP repertoire (Rodriguez et al., 2013); we found that treating BMDM with purified PIM6 similarly induced the early and late response genes in a TLR2-dependent manner (Figure 4E–F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E–F and citation to Rodriguez et al., 2013

claim: The two observed components of the TLR2-dependent response to Mtb infection reflect inherent dynamics of TLR2 signaling in macrophages rather than dynamics specific to recognition of intact Mtb.
source: The two observed components of the TLR2-dependent response to Mtb infection thus appear to reflect inherent dynamics of TLR2 signaling in macrophages rather than dynamics specific to recognition of intact Mtb
evidence: Inferred from the observation that synthetic TLR2 ligands produce similar biphasic responses

claim: None of the known adapters TRIF, TRAM, or TIRAP were required for induction of the late response.
source: None of the known adapters TRIF, TRAM, or TIRAP were required for induction of the late response (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D

claim: Late response component genes were expressed similarly in wild-type and TNF receptor knockout BMDM.
source: We first considered that expression of genes in the later component may be driven by signaling through the TNF receptor initiated by the early component; however, late response component genes were expressed similarly in wild-type and TNF receptor knockout BMDM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: PAM3CSK4-induced expression of genes in the early cluster was not significantly changed by dynasore pre-treatment.
source: PAM3CSK4-induced expression of genes in the early cluster was not significantly changed by dynasore pre-treatment (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: PAM3CSK4-induced expression of genes in the late cluster was markedly reduced by dynasore pre-treatment.
source: In contrast, PAM3CSK4-induced expression of genes in the late cluster was markedly reduced (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Dynasore significantly decreased Mtb uptake.
source: The effect of dynasore on Mtb uptake has not previously been tested; using gentamicin protection assays, we found that dynasore significantly decreased Mtb uptake (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C

claim: Inhibition of Mtb uptake with dynasore left expression of genes in the early TLR2-dependent cluster largely preserved.
source: Similar to treatment with synthetic ligand, inhibition of Mtb uptake with dynasore left expression of genes in the early TLR2-dependent cluster largely preserved (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Inhibition of Mtb uptake with dynasore significantly blunted expression of genes in the late cluster.
source: Similar to treatment with synthetic ligand, inhibition of Mtb uptake with dynasore left expression of genes in the early TLR2-dependent cluster largely preserved (Figure 5C), but significantly blunted expression of genes in the late cluster (Figure 5D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Dynasore pre-treatment had minimal impact on TNF release.
source: Similar to the patterns observed for Tnf transcription, dynasore pre-treatment had minimal impact on TNF release (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5F

claim: Expression of early cluster genes can be initiated from the plasma membrane.
source: These results suggest that while expression of early cluster genes can be initiated from the plasma membrane, expression of genes in the later cluster is dependent upon endosomal uptake
evidence: Inferred from the observation that dynasore does not affect early gene expression

claim: Expression of genes in the later cluster is dependent upon endosomal uptake.
source: These results suggest that while expression of early cluster genes can be initiated from the plasma membrane, expression of genes in the later cluster is dependent upon endosomal uptake
evidence: Inferred from the observation that dynasore blocks late gene expression

claim: Stimulation of BMDM with TLR2 agonists modestly induced type I IFNs.
source: We found that stimulation of BMDM with TLR2 agonists modestly induced type I IFNs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B

claim: Type I IFN induction by TLR2 agonists was dependent upon TLR2.
source: this induction was dependent upon TLR2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C

claim: Type I IFN induction by TLR2 agonists was partially inhibited by dynasore pre-treatment.
source: this induction was dependent upon TLR2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C) and partially inhibited by dynasore pre-treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D

claim: The kinetics and magnitude of induction of Ifnb1 were distinct from the late pro-inflammatory component of the TLR2 response.
source: However, the kinetics and magnitude of induction of Ifnb1 were distinct from the late pro-inflammatory component of the TLR2 response, suggesting that the endosome-specific pro-inflammatory response is distinct from the type I IFN response
evidence: Inferred from comparison of temporal expression patterns

claim: Induction of the type I IFN response to Mtb was independent of TLR2.
source: Consistent with established models, induction of the type I IFN response to Mtb was independent of TLR2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and consistency with established models

claim: PDIM and ESX-1 are required for induction of the type I IFN response to Mtb.
source: Both PDIM and ESX-1 are required for induction of the type I IFN response to Mtb (Barczak et al., 2017; Stanley et al., 2007; Figure 5—figure supplement 2F)
evidence: Supported by citations to Barczak et al., 2017; Stanley et al., 2007 and data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F

claim: STING is strictly required for the type I IFN response to Mtb upstream of IRF3 activation.
source: STING is strictly required for the type I IFN response to Mtb upstream of IRF3 activation (Manzanillo et al., 2012; Figure 5—figure supplement 2E)
evidence: Supported by citation to Manzanillo et al., 2012 and data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E

claim: The mechanism through which PDIM and ESX-1 blunt the TLR2-dependent response to Mtb is independent of their role in type I IFN induction.
source: In fact, neither prediction tested correct (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G), suggesting that the mechanism through which PDIM and ESX-1 blunt the TLR2-dependent response to Mtb is independent of their role in type I IFN induction
evidence: Inferred from experimental data in Sting-/- BMDM shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2G

claim: Candida-mediated phagosomal membrane damage interferes with phagosome acidification.
source: Candida-mediated phagosomal membrane damage and sterile phagosomal membrane damage have both been described to interfere with phagosome acidification, potentially because of loss of the proton gradient across the membrane at sites of damage (Eriksson et al., 2020; Westman et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Eriksson et al., 2020; Westman et al., 2018

claim: An ESX-1 mutant in Mycobacterium marinum resides in a more highly acidified macrophage phagosome than wild-type M. marinum.
source: An ESX-1 mutant in Mycobacterium marinum has in fact previously been shown to reside in a more highly acidified macrophage phagosome than wild-type M. marinum (Tan et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tan et al., 2006

claim: Inhibitors of phagosome acidification limit the MYD88-dependent response to S. aureus.
source: Providing suggestive evidence for a link between phagosome acidification and the TLR2 response, inhibitors of phagosome acidification limit the MYD88-dependent response to S. aureus (Ip et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ip et al., 2010

claim: pHrodo mean fluorescent intensity around PDIM- or ESX-1-mutant Mtb was significantly higher than around wild-type Mtb at 6, 12, or 24 hr post-infection.
source: At 6, 12, or 24 hr post-infection, pHrodo mean fluorescent intensity around PDIM- or ESX-1-mutant Mtb was significantly higher than around wild-type Mtb (Figure 6A)
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Phagosomes containing PDIM- or ESX-1-mutant Mtb become relatively more acidic than phagosomes containing wild-type Mtb.
source: At 6, 12, or 24 hr post-infection, pHrodo mean fluorescent intensity around PDIM- or ESX-1-mutant Mtb was significantly higher than around wild-type Mtb (Figure 6A), suggesting that phagosomes containing PDIM- or ESX-1-mutant Mtb becomes relatively more acidic than phagosomes containing wild-type Mtb
evidence: Inferred from pHrodo fluorescence data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Pre-treatment with concanamycin A limits phagosome acidification in BMDM.
source: We first confirmed that pre-treatment with concanamycin A, which inhibits the vacuolar ATPase, limits phagosome acidification in BMDM using both zymosan beads (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) and infection with pHrodo-labeled PDIM and ESX-1 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and 1D

claim: Expression of the early cluster of genes was not significantly changed by concanamycin A pre-treatment during Mtb infection.
source: We found that while expression of the early cluster of genes was not significantly changed (Figure 6B), expression of the second cluster of genes was markedly diminished in the presence of concanamycin A (Figure 6C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Expression of the second cluster of genes was markedly diminished in the presence of concanamycin A during Mtb infection.
source: We found that while expression of the early cluster of genes was not significantly changed (Figure 6B), expression of the second cluster of genes was markedly diminished in the presence of concanamycin A (Figure 6C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Phagosome acidification enhances the endosomal component of the TLR2-dependent response to Mtb.
source: These results suggested that phagosome acidification enhances the endosomal component of the TLR2-dependent response to Mtb
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking acidification reduces late gene expression

claim: Expression of genes in the early component of the response to synthetic TLR2 ligand was not changed by the addition of concanamycin A.
source: Expression of genes in the early component of the response to synthetic TLR2 ligand was not changed by the addition of concanamycin A (Figure 6D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Expression of genes in the later component of the response to synthetic TLR2 ligand was markedly diminished by the addition of concanamycin A.
source: However, expression of genes in the later component of the response was markedly diminished by the addition of concanamycin A (Figure 6E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E

claim: The late component of TLR2 signaling is dependent on phagosome acidification independent of the capacity to process pathogen and release TLR2 agonists.
source: These results suggest that the late component of TLR2 signaling is dependent on phagosome acidification entirely independent of the capacity to process pathogen and release TLR2 agonists
evidence: Inferred from the observation that synthetic ligands also require acidification for late response

claim: Mtb-mediated damage of the phagosome membrane blunts the endosome-specific TLR2 response by limiting phagosome acidification.
source: Taken together, our results are consistent with the hypothesis that Mtb-mediated damage of the phagosome membrane blunts the endosome-specific TLR2 response by limiting phagosome acidification
evidence: Inferred from combined experimental data on phagosome pH and TLR2 responses

claim: Signaling of the endosome-restricted TLRs, TLR7, and TLR9 is strictly dependent upon endosomal acid-activated proteases.
source: Signaling of the endosome-restricted TLRs, TLR7, and TLR9 is in fact strictly dependent upon endosomal acid-activated proteases (Ewald et al., 2008; Park et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Ewald et al., 2008; Park et al., 2008

claim: Mtb infection drives macrophage cell death, including apoptosis.
source: Mtb infection has been shown to drive macrophage cell death, including apoptosis (Keane et al., 1997)
evidence: Supported by citation to Keane et al., 1997

claim: Mtb infection drives macrophage necrosis.
source: Mtb infection has been shown to drive macrophage cell death, including apoptosis (Keane et al., 1997), necrosis (Danelishvili et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Danelishvili et al., 2003

claim: Mtb infection drives macrophage ferroptosis.
source: Mtb infection has been shown to drive macrophage cell death, including apoptosis (Keane et al., 1997), necrosis (Danelishvili et al., 2003), and ferroptosis (Amaral et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Amaral et al., 2019

claim: PDIM contributes to macrophage necrosis.
source: PDIM has been described to specifically contribute to macrophage necrosis (Quigley et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Quigley et al., 2017

claim: ESX-1 contributes to macrophage cell death after infection.
source: ESX-1 has also been shown to contribute to macrophage cell death after infection (Augenstreich et al., 2017; Derrick and Morris, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Augenstreich et al., 2017; Derrick and Morris, 2007

claim: Pre-treatment of macrophages with a TLR4 or TLR2 agonist reduced Mtb-induced cell death.
source: In one study, pre-treatment of macrophages with a TLR4 or TLR2 agonist reduced Mtb-induced cell death (Rojas et al., 1997)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rojas et al., 1997

claim: In wild-type macrophages PDIM and ESX-1 mutants induced less cell death than wild-type Mtb or complemented mutants.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we found that in wild-type macrophages PDIM and ESX-1 mutants induced less cell death than wild-type Mtb or complemented mutants (Figure 7A–B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A–B

claim: Infection with wild-type Mtb induced a similar degree of cell death in wild-type and Tlr2-/- macrophages.
source: Infection with wild-type Mtb induced a similar degree of cell death in wild-type and Tlr2-/- macrophages
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing cell death in different macrophage genotypes

claim: The resistance to cell death observed in wild-type macrophages infected with PDIM or ESX-1 mutants was partially lost in Tlr2-/- macrophages.
source: However, the resistance to cell death observed in wild-type macrophages infected with PDIM or ESX-1 mutants was partially lost in Tlr2-/- macrophages (Figure 7A–B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A–B

claim: PDIM and ESX-1 interference with TLR2-dependent responses contributes to macrophage cell death following infection.
source: These results suggest that PDIM and ESX-1 interference with TLR2-dependent responses contributes to macrophage cell death following infection
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mutant attenuation is partially lost in Tlr2-/- macrophages

claim: PDIM and ESX-1 mutants grew less well than wild-type Mtb in C57BL/6J BMDM.
source: As expected, PDIM and ESX-1 mutants grew less well than wild-type Mtb in C57BL/6J BMDM (Figure 7C)
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Growth of wild-type Mtb was modestly enhanced in Tlr2-/- macrophages relative to wild-type macrophages.
source: Growth of wild-type Mtb was modestly enhanced in Tlr2-/- macrophages relative to wild-type macrophages
evidence: Supported by CFU data comparing growth in different macrophage genotypes

claim: The PDIM and ESX-1 mutants grew significantly more robustly in the Tlr2-/- BMDM than in wild-type BMDM, with growth similar to wild-type Mtb.
source: further, the PDIM and ESX-1 mutants grew significantly more robustly in the Tlr2-/- BMDM than in wild-type BMDM, with growth similar to wild-type Mtb (Figure 7C)
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 7C

claim: TLR2-dependent responses contribute to growth restriction of the PDIM and ESX-1 mutants in macrophages.
source: These results suggest that TLR2-dependent responses contribute to growth restriction of the PDIM and ESX-1 mutants in macrophages
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mutants grow better in Tlr2-/- macrophages

claim: PDIM and ESX-1-mediated interference with TLR2-dependent responses contributes to the pathogenesis of Mtb infection in macrophages.
source: Together with our macrophage survival data, these results indicate that PDIM and ESX-1-mediated interference with TLR2-dependent responses contributes to the pathogenesis of Mtb infection in macrophages
evidence: Inferred from combined data on cell survival and bacterial growth

claim: Some studies have shown a modest increase in Mtb growth in Tlr2-/- mice relative to wild-type mice.
source: Some studies have shown a modest increase in Mtb growth in Tlr2-/- mice relative to wild-type mice (Drennan et al., 2004; McBride et al., 2011; McBride et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Drennan et al., 2004; McBride et al., 2011; McBride et al., 2013

claim: Most studies have shown increased lung pathology in Tlr2-/- mice, with larger infiltrates, less organization, and more inflammatory cells.
source: Most studies have shown increased lung pathology in Tlr2-/- mice, with larger infiltrates, less organization, and more inflammatory cells described as key features in various studies (Drennan et al., 2004; McBride et al., 2013; Bafica et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to Drennan et al., 2004; McBride et al., 2013; Bafica et al., 2005

claim: Tlr2-/- mice have increased Mtb dissemination to liver and spleen.
source: Tlr2-/- mice have been shown to have increased Mtb dissemination to liver and spleen (Drennan et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Drennan et al., 2004

claim: Tlr2-/- mice have a more rapid progression to death following Mtb infection.
source: Tlr2-/- mice have been shown to have increased Mtb dissemination to liver and spleen (Drennan et al., 2004) and a more rapid progression to death following infection (Drennan et al., 2004; Bafica et al., 2005; Reiling et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to Drennan et al., 2004; Bafica et al., 2005; Reiling et al., 2002

claim: TLR2 plays a somewhat modest role in host control of TB infection.
source: In aggregate, these data suggest that TLR2 plays a somewhat modest role in host control of TB infection
evidence: Inferred from review of published literature on TLR2 knockout mice

claim: PDIM-mutant Mtb growth was restricted relative to wild-type Mtb growth in C57BL/6J mice at 6 weeks post-infection.
source: At the 6 week timepoint, as expected, PDIM-mutant Mtb growth was restricted relative to wild-type Mtb growth in C57BL/6J mice
evidence: Supported by CFU data from mouse infections

claim: Wild-type Mtb grew similarly in the lungs of C57BL/6J and Tlr2-/- mice.
source: Wild-type Mtb grew similarly in the lungs of C57BL/6J and Tlr2-/- mice
evidence: Supported by CFU data from mouse infections

claim: PDIM-mutant Mtb had increased growth in the lungs of Tlr2-/- mice relative to C57BL/6J mice.
source: In contrast, PDIM-mutant Mtb had increased growth in the lungs of Tlr2-/- mice relative to C57BL/6J mice (Figure 7D)
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 7D

claim: PDIM-mediated interference with activation of components of the TLR2-dependent response contributes to the capacity of the bacterium to grow in lung.
source: PDIM-mutant Mtb had increased growth in the lungs of Tlr2-/- mice relative to C57BL/6J mice (Figure 7D), suggesting that PDIM-mediated interference with activation of components of the TLR2-dependent response contributes to the capacity of the bacterium to grow in lung
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PDIM mutant grows better in Tlr2-/- mice

claim: Lungs of C57BL/6J mice infected with wild-type Mtb demonstrated defined areas of inflammation by 6 weeks post-infection.
source: Histopathologically, the lungs of C57BL/6J mice infected with wild-type Mtb demonstrated defined areas of inflammation by 6 weeks post-infection (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: Lungs of C57BL/6J mice infected with PDIM-mutant Mtb showed trends toward fewer areas of inflammation and smaller lesion sizes.
source: Lungs of C57BL/6J mice infected with PDIM-mutant Mtb showed trends toward fewer areas of inflammation and smaller lesion sizes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: In Tlr2-/- mutant mice infected with PDIM-mutant Mtb, infiltrates showed a trend toward more numerous and larger areas of involvement than was observed in C57BL/6J mice.
source: In Tlr2-/- mutant mice infected with PDIM-mutant Mtb, infiltrates showed a trend toward more numerous and larger areas of involvement than was observed in C57BL/6J mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–C)
evidence: Supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–C

claim: PDIM modulation of TLR2-dependent responses contributes to pathogenesis in vivo.
source: In total, our data suggest that PDIM modulation of TLR2-dependent responses contributes to pathogenesis in vivo
evidence: Inferred from combined data on bacterial growth and histopathology in mice

claim: Growth of the PDIM mutant is only partially restored in Tlr2-/- mice, indicating that additional mechanisms contribute to the attenuation of PDIM mutants in vivo.
source: Growth of the PDIM mutant is only partially restored in Tlr2-/- mice, indicating that additional mechanisms contribute to the attenuation of PDIM mutants in vivo
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PDIM mutant growth is not fully restored to wild-type levels in Tlr2-/- mice

claim: TLR2 can signal from the plasma membrane and endosomes, similar to TLR4.
source: TLR2, a receptor for bacterial cell wall lipoproteins, has been suggested to signal from the plasma membrane and endosomes, similar to TLR4
evidence: Based on established knowledge about TLR2 signaling

claim: TNF release in response to S. aureus was shown to be partially dependent upon TLR2 and dependent upon endosomal uptake.
source: Endosome-specific TLR2 signaling in response to pathogenic bacteria has been partially explored using the model of Staphylococcus aureus taken up into macrophages (Ip et al., 2010); in that work, TNF release was shown to be partially dependent upon TLR2 and dependent upon endosomal uptake
evidence: Supported by citation to Ip et al., 2010

claim: TLR2 activation induces a type I interferon (IFN) transcriptional response from endosomes.
source: TLR2 activation has also been described to induce a type I interferon (IFN) transcriptional response from endosomes (Barbalat et al., 2009; Dietrich et al., 2010; Musilova et al., 2019; Stack et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Barbalat et al., 2009; Dietrich et al., 2010; Musilova et al., 2019; Stack et al., 2014

claim: Mtb has a complex repertoire of PAMPs, and infection with Mtb is recognized by both membrane-bound and cytosolic PRRs.
source: Mtb has a complex repertoire of PAMPs, and infection with Mtb is recognized by both membrane-bound and cytosolic PRRs
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Mtb recognition

claim: The canonical Mtb virulence factors phthiocerol dimycocerosate (PDIM) and ESX-1 contribute to disruption of the macrophage phagosomal membrane upon infection.
source: The canonical Mtb virulence factors phthiocerol dimycocerosate (PDIM) and ESX-1 contribute to disruption of the macrophage phagosomal membrane upon infection (Augenstreich et al., 2017; Barczak et al., 2017; Manzanillo et al., 2012; Quigley et al., 2017; Simeone et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Augenstreich et al., 2017; Barczak et al., 2017; Manzanillo et al., 2012; Quigley et al., 2017; Simeone et al., 2012

claim: PDIM and ESX-1 functions blunt induction of an inflammatory transcriptional program that includes multiple genes individually linked to control of tuberculosis (TB) infection.
source: These results suggest that PDIM and ESX-1 functions blunt induction of an inflammatory transcriptional program that includes multiple genes individually linked to control of tuberculosis (TB) infection
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing enhanced expression of host-protective genes in response to mutants

claim: PDIM and ESX-1 contribute to Mtb virulence in part by blunting a protective endosome-specific component of the TLR2-dependent response to infection.
source: These results support a model in which PDIM and ESX-1 contribute to Mtb virulence in part by blunting a protective endosome-specific component of the TLR2-dependent response to infection
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental data on TLR2 responses, phagosome acidification, and infection outcomes

claim: TLR2 activation drives distinct compartment-specific pro-inflammatory transcriptional responses, reflected in both the sets of genes expressed and the kinetics of induction.
source: Our results support a model in which TLR2 activation in fact drives distinct compartment-specific pro-inflammatory transcriptional responses, reflected in both the sets of genes expressed and the kinetics of induction
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental data showing spatial and temporal differences in TLR2 responses

claim: TNF is critical for infection control in TB.
source: In the case of TB, TNF, a component of the early response, is known to be critical for infection control
evidence: Based on established knowledge about TNF in TB

claim: The later TLR2 response component includes expression of multiple genes demonstrated to be important for both cell intrinsic control of Mtb and priming of the adaptive immune response.
source: However, the later response component includes expression of multiple genes demonstrated to be important for both cell intrinsic control of Mtb and priming of the adaptive immune response
evidence: Based on citations to literature about individual genes in subcluster 1B

claim: Undermining the second component of the TLR2 response contributes to Mtb's success as a pathogen.
source: Our results demonstrating an interaction between TLR2 and PDIM or ESX-1 for infection outcome suggest that undermining this second component contributes to Mtb's success as a pathogen
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on infection outcomes in macrophages and mice

claim: PDIM interferes with an effective MYD88 inflammatory response, as measured by the outcomes of macrophage recruitment to M. marinum-containing lesions in vivo and iNOS production.
source: PDIM has previously been shown to interfere with an effective MYD88 inflammatory response, as measured by the outcomes of macrophage recruitment to M. marinum-containing lesions in vivo and iNOS production (Cambier et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cambier et al., 2014

claim: The secreted hydrolase Hip1 blunts the secretion of cytokines, including TNF, following infection.
source: The secreted hydrolase Hip1 has been shown to blunt the secretion of cytokines, including TNF, following infection (Madan-Lala et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Madan-Lala et al., 2011

claim: The surface lipid sulfolipid-1 interferes with surface recognition of TLR2 agonists.
source: Recently, the surface lipid sulfolipid-1 was shown to interfere with surface recognition of TLR2 agonists (Blanc et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Blanc et al., 2017

claim: Mycobacteria have evolved multiple strategies to undermine TLR2 activation from both the surface and endosome.
source: In aggregate, these results suggest that mycobacteria have evolved multiple strategies to undermine TLR2 activation from both the surface and endosome
evidence: Inferred from the combined evidence of multiple interference mechanisms

claim: TLR2 activation can dampen IFN-dependent gene expression and cell functions.
source: Adding to the complexity of TLR2-dependent phenotypes in TB infection, studies of the relationship between Mtb TLR2 agonists and IFN-dependent functions have shown that TLR2 activation can dampen IFN-dependent gene expression and cell functions (Pecora et al., 2006; Banaiee et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to Pecora et al., 2006; Banaiee et al., 2006
